summary: Updates RFC 2131 to fix an issue with its rule that a DHCP server must not return the client identifier option to the client. The document addresses problems that rule caused, allowing servers to echo the option in replies.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6842 changes DHCP so a server returns the client identifier when the client included it in a request. The client checks that the returned identifier matches its own before accepting the reply.

subtitle: DHCP servers must return a client identifier when the client sent one.

tldr.problem: Clients with no usable hardware address may rely on a client identifier, but replies that omit it can be dropped or misidentified.
tldr.mechanism: When the request includes a client identifier, the server returns it unchanged and the client discards a reply containing a different identifier.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 2131 to make client-to-reply matching clearer, including when the hardware address field is zero.
tldr.outcomeLabel: Match the reply to the client

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 6842's status as Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 2131's DHCP client-identifier handling rules.

sections.title: Why Replies Need the Client Identifier
sections.content:
DHCP uses the client identifier or hardware address together with the assigned network address to identify a client's lease. Earlier DHCP rules said that a server must not return the client identifier in DHCPOFFER or DHCPACK messages.

Some clients may have no valid hardware address and set chaddr to zero. If a reply omits the client identifier in that case, a relay may drop it or the client may be unable to tell that the reply is intended for it.
sections.plainLanguage: A client may need its identifier to recognize its DHCP reply, especially when it has no hardware address to send. Leaving the identifier out can make the reply ambiguous.

sections.title: Echoing and Checking the Identifier
sections.content:
If a client sends a client identifier option, the DHCP server must return the same option unaltered in its response. If the client did not send one, the server must not include one in its response.

When a client receives a DHCP message with a client identifier, it must compare that value with the identifier it is configured to send. If they do not match, it silently discards the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The server repeats the identifier the client supplied. The client checks the returned value and ignores the reply if it belongs to a different identifier.

sections.title: The Change to RFC 2131
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 2131 by changing the rule about returning a client identifier. The identifier is required in DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK, and DHCPNAK responses when it was sent by the client, and must not be included when the client did not send it.

The memo notes that the earlier omission rule was intended to conserve packet space. It judges the benefit of returning the identifier to outweigh the small risk that a client might reject an option it did not previously expect.
sections.plainLanguage: The server's reply now carries the identifier when the request carried it. This helps both relays and clients match a reply to the right client.
